description: SOLUS — Latin for alone; solitary; on one's own.
summary: SOLUS is an interactive scientific map that helps astronauts plan crewed-rover drives and Marswalks on Mars. Users pick a region, draw a route, and SOLUS returns numbered risk points (steep slopes, crater rims, data gaps), each with its coordinates, measured value and the NASA data behind it. All terrain analysis is computed from 20 NASA Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter elevation models (HiRISE and CTX), and we validated our slopes against the tilt actually recorded by the Perseverance and Curiosity rovers: they agree within about 1–2 degrees on average. SOLUS never calls a route "safe": unknown terrain is shown as unknown, and every warning traces back to real data, a stated resolution and an explicit calculation.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

SOLUS is a 2D "Google Maps for exploring Mars" for planning crewed-rover drives and Marswalks. It covers three regions chosen by data quality, not fame: Jezero crater, Gale crater and West Candor Chasma.

- Plan a route by clicking waypoints. SOLUS samples the terrain along it and lists numbered risks: caution and no-go slopes, crater-rim crossings, stretches with no elevation data, and areas outside any elevation model.

- Each risk card shows coordinates, the measured value, the source camera and dataset, the measurement baseline, a 1–6 severity score and a plain-language evidence sentence.

- Route summary: distance, estimated travel time, maximum slope, climb/descent, an elevation profile, and a walk-back warning when the route goes beyond the distance a crew could walk back to shelter.

- Two mission modes: Rover (caution ≥15°, no-go ≥25°, 10 km walk-back) and Marswalk (caution ≥15°, no-go ≥20°, 2 km walk-back). Thresholds come from NASA sources: Apollo Lunar Roving Vehicle performance, Mars rover operating limits, and NASA's Artemis spacesuit requirement.

- Layers: NASA imagery, slope, geology, craters, real rover traverses, no-data areas, flagged suspect values and elevation-model coverage. Click anywhere to inspect slope, elevation, geologic unit and nearby hazards.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Data selection: we ranked locations by the overlap of NASA elevation data and imagery, then chose three regions.

2. Offline processing (Python): for each of 20 elevation models from NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (HiRISE and CTX cameras) we computed slope (Horn method), roughness, relief, data gaps and outliers, separately in each model's own projection. We never stitched models together (overlapping models disagree by tens of metres), never filled missing data, and flagged suspicious values instead of deleting them. HiRISE slope uses a 5 m baseline, about a rover's length, to remove pixel noise; CTX uses 18 m.

3. Validation: we compared our slopes with the on-board tilt NASA recorded at Perseverance's and Curiosity's waypoints. Median differences were 0.1–1.9°. Our Rover-mode limits rate 97–99.9% of the distance those rovers actually drove as passable. HiRISE and CTX agree on average (median difference under 0.6°).

4. Web app (HTML/CSS/JavaScript): a lightweight Mars map engine on the Mars 2000 sphere, streaming NASA Mars Trek imagery and sampling the pre-computed terrain grids along any route the user draws.

BENEFITS

- Scientific honesty: every warning traces back to NASA data and a stated calculation; unknown terrain is never presented as safe; limitations are shown openly in the app.

- Fast planning: route-level risk in seconds instead of manual image inspection.

- Adaptable: the same pipeline can process any region covered by NASA elevation data.

INTENDED IMPACT

Help mission planners and future crews choose data-backed traverses, and show clearly where more data (higher-resolution imaging, soil information) is needed before humans go.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

- It checks itself against reality: slopes are validated against the tilt real Mars rovers recorded while driving.

- It treats "we don't know" as information: data gaps are mapped and counted, never hidden or guessed.

- It turns raw orbital elevation data into plain-language evidence a crew can act on, with a separate mode for walking astronauts.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Data quality over fame when choosing regions.

- Measurement scale: 1 m slopes are noisy, so we use a 5 m baseline close to a vehicle's length.

- No published slope limit exists for crewed Mars rovers or walking on Mars, so we use NASA lunar and robotic-rover limits and state this openly.

- Slope cannot show sand versus rock, and rocks under about 1 m are not visible in the data; the app says so.

- Different elevation models disagree in absolute height, so elevation change is only counted within one model.

TOOLS

Python (NumPy, SciPy, Rasterio, GDAL, Shapely, pyproj, Pillow, Matplotlib); HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no frameworks; NASA/JPL Mars Trek map tiles; Playwright for automated testing; AI assistants (Claude, ChatGPT) for coding, processing and research. Built solo by team SOLUS.
